\section{Introduction}
Whether moving to a low-poverty neighbourhood improves
children's schooling remains contested.
Experimental evidence from housing vouchers points to
sizeable gains for children who moved young \cite{chetty2016},
while quasi-experimental estimates are more mixed
\cite[chapter~4]{sampson2012}.
We revisit the question with administrative records
from a municipal mobility programme.

\section{Discussion}
The estimated effects are concentrated among children
below the age of ten at the time of the move,
a pattern consistent with the exposure hypothesis
\cite{wodtke2011}.
Selection into destinations remains the central threat;
our within-family estimates address it directly
\cite{holland2019}.
That the gains appear only after four years of exposure
echoes the long-run follow-ups of earlier experiments
\cite{ludwig2013}.

Experimental evidence from housing vouchers points to
sizeable gains for children who moved young \citep{chetty2016},
while quasi-experimental estimates are more mixed
\citep[chapter~4]{sampson2012}.
We revisit the question with administrative records

The estimated effects are concentrated among children
below the age of ten at the time of the move,
